name: Token
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Riding on Someone Else's Rails
lesson.summary: A token is a digital asset created and tracked by a smart contract on top of an existing blockchain, distinct from that blockchain's own native currency, and far cheaper to create than building a new blockchain from scratch.
lesson.body:
Most blockchains have a native currency baked directly into their protocol, used to pay for transactions and, on proof-of-work networks, to reward miners. Ethereum has ether, Bitcoin has bitcoin. A token is something different: it is an asset that does not have its own independent blockchain at all, but instead exists as an entry tracked by a smart contract deployed on top of an existing blockchain, borrowing that underlying chain's security and consensus rather than building its own from the ground up.

This relationship depends directly on the blockchain definition covered earlier: because the underlying ledger is a shared, ordered, tamper-evident record that every participating node verifies, anything recorded correctly on it, including a smart contract's internal bookkeeping of who owns how much of some token, inherits those same guarantees. A token contract typically does nothing more exotic than maintain an internal mapping from addresses to balances, and update that mapping whenever it receives a transaction instructing it to transfer some amount from one address to another. The blockchain does not need to know or care what the token represents; it just needs to correctly execute and permanently record the contract's instructions.

Why bother creating a token instead of a whole new blockchain? Building and, more importantly, securing an entirely new blockchain from scratch requires recruiting a large, distributed set of participants willing to run nodes and, on proof-of-work systems, dedicate real mining resources to defending it, which is an enormous undertaking. Deploying a token contract on an already-secure, already-established blockchain like Ethereum sidesteps almost all of that. A single developer can deploy a functioning token in an afternoon, immediately benefiting from the thousands of nodes already securing the underlying chain.

This ease of creation is precisely why tokens have been used to represent an enormous range of things: a stablecoin pegged to a national currency, a governance right entitling holders to vote on a protocol's future changes, a loyalty point system, a claim on a share of some project's future revenue, or a ticket granting access to some service. The token itself is just a balance in a contract's internal ledger; what that balance is understood to represent is a matter of the surrounding project's design and, often, its legal and marketing claims rather than anything enforced by the blockchain itself.

A concrete illustration: a project wanting to distribute ownership stakes to early contributors does not need to build a payment network, a distributed set of validating nodes, or a consensus mechanism. It deploys a token contract on an existing chain, mints some initial supply to specified addresses, and from that point forward every transfer of that token is simply a transaction calling that contract's transfer function, recorded on the underlying blockchain exactly like any other transaction, inheriting its permanence and public verifiability without the project ever having built any blockchain infrastructure of its own.
